sections.h2: Who bills and who taxes in Boone County
sections.html:
The county Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values each parcel, the Boone County Sheriff bills and collects, and several overlapping districts levy the tax. The PVA sets the assessment as of January 1, and the sheriff mails the bill in the fall.

Your bill adds a state rate, a county rate, a city rate where one applies, and separate rates for the library, health department, extension office, fire district and school district. Neighbors can owe different totals if their parcels fall in different districts. Most of the county belongs to Boone County Schools, and a portion lies in the Walton-Verona Independent district, so the school share depends on the parcel.

Ask which year you owe. Kentucky taxes follow the January 1 owner, so a bill that shows up in September or October may carry the name of whoever held the house in January.

Boone's sheriff runs four payment stages, and they repeat annually because KRS 134.015 fixes the pattern, barring a delayed schedule approved by the state.

Boone County Sheriff collection stages
StageDatesWhat you pay
DiscountOctober 1 to November 1Bill minus 2 percent
Face amountNovember 2 to December 31The printed amount
First penaltyJanuary 1 to 31Printed amount plus 5 percent
Second penaltyFebruary 1 to April 15Penalty of 10 percent, plus the sheriff's 10 percent add-on

Because partial payments are refused, a bill is paid in one lump. Card payments online add a vendor charge, and e-checks add a smaller flat charge. The sheriff's office is on Conrad Lane in Burlington, with Saturday hours in October, and bills go in the mail before the end of September. The sheriff also listed Heritage Bank branches as places to pay.

sections.h2: A bill still open in April
sections.html:
If a bill remains unpaid at the close of business on April 15, the sheriff passes it to the County Clerk, and a lien is recorded. From there the account picks up a 20 percent attorney fee, a 10 percent clerk fee and interest at 1 percent monthly, and the debt may be sold to a private buyer the next summer.

  • The lien stays on the parcel for up to 11 years under KRS 134.015, no matter who buys the house.
  • Warnings go to the owner of record, so a stale mailing address can hide them.
  • The county attorney can arrange an installment plan.

A parcel with an open certificate can still be sold. The seller's share covers the payoff, and the clerk quotes it, not the sheriff.

The PVA is step one, since no formal appeal is accepted before you have met with that office, and Boone's online request form is open from October 1 to May 1. You can also email appeals@boonecountyky.org to book the meeting.

The window is short. The tax roll sits open for inspection for two weeks beginning in the first week of May. If the meeting doesn't settle the value, you file with the County Clerk by the next business day after that window ends. A bill itself can't be appealed, because values must be final before rates are calculated.

  • Comparable sale prices from homes near yours are the strongest evidence, and the PVA's own model works from the same kind of data.
  • Photos or repair estimates help when the house is in worse shape than the record says.
  • Request the list of sales behind your parcel's value.

The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after inspection closes, under KRS 133.030. If you still disagree, its decision letter explains the next appeal step.

sections.h2: Why did my assessment go up?
sections.html:
Sales drive most increases. The PVA values homes from nearby arm's length transactions through a computer-assisted system, and every parcel gets a physical look within four years, so a jump often means several years of price growth arriving at once.

House Bill 44 caps growth in countywide tax revenue at 4 percent a year. That law acts on the tax rate, not the assessed value, so a rising valuation can come alongside a falling rate. Kentucky requires the PVA's values to land within 90 to 110 percent of sales prices, and a yearly ratio study tests it.

Boone had 135,968 residents in 2020 and an estimated 145,316 by July 2025, up 6.9 percent, across 56,021 housing units. Half of owner-occupied homes are worth more than $277,300, and median household income is $99,414.

Homeowners turning 65 during the tax year, and those totally disabled, receive a flat deduction from assessed value. The PVA lists $49,100 for 2026, and the amount should print on the face of your bill once the PVA holds your form.

  • You must own the house and live there on January 1.
  • A household gets one deduction, even when both spouses meet the age test.
  • Disabled owners under 65 renew every year, unless the disability is a service-connected rating or a permanent finding by Social Security or a state retirement system.
  • The deduction belongs to the owner. After a sale the PVA lifts it from the old address, and the buyer applies on their own.

If the amount is missing, call the PVA before you pay. KRS 132.810 allows a refund for late approval, though fixing it first is simpler. Forms go in by mail, fax, email or the PVA's online form.

The usual practice is for the closing agent to pay the year's tax from the seller's funds and divide it by days of ownership. A bill for a house bought after January 1 may still arrive in the former owner's name, so the settlement statement is where the split gets recorded.

Three checks help. Find out whether this year's bill is paid, and ask the sheriff for a duplicate if yours never came, since that office can't see new deeds. Make sure a recorded deed or other document updates the owner name at the PVA, because name changes happen there. For an inherited house, the PVA accepts a death certificate to update the record.

Owners with a delinquent bill, a missing exemption or deferred repairs sometimes pick a direct sale to a cash buyer, who purchases the house in its present condition, with the tax payoff deducted at closing.

The cycle touches four offices. The PVA in Burlington values property and takes exemption forms and appeal requests at 859-334-2181. The sheriff collects bills at 859-334-2175, with an online portal at boonecountytax.com. The County Clerk files deeds, receives appeals and holds the bills that go delinquent in April.

faqs.q: What dates matter for a Boone County bill?
faqs.a: Four stages apply each year. Paying by November 1 earns the 2 percent discount, the printed amount holds through December, and a bill still unpaid at the end of January moves to the larger penalty stage.

faqs.q: Can a Boone County assessment be appealed after the bill arrives?
faqs.a: No. Appeals belong to the May inspection period. Meet with the PVA first, then file with the county clerk by the next business day after the period closes.

faqs.q: How large is the Boone County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: The PVA lists $49,100 for 2026. It comes off the assessment, not the bill, and applies to owners turning 65 in the tax year or totally disabled.

faqs.q: Who receives the bill if I sold my Boone County house during the year?
faqs.a: The bill goes to whoever owned on January 1. The buyer should forward it or call the sheriff for a copy, and the settlement statement divides the cost.

faqs.q: Is a Boone County home with back taxes still sellable?
faqs.a: Yes. A lien attaches to the parcel, so the unpaid amount and any clerk and attorney fees come out of what the seller receives. Request an exact payoff from the sheriff or clerk before choosing an asking price.
